item.title: Be careful when posting on LinkedIn because...
item.description:
…now you need to comply with EU AI Act (article 50)

For scientists posting about their research on LinkedIn, Article 50 of the EU AI Act applies directly if they use AI to generate or manipulate their posts, unless they meet specific, strict exceptions.

IMPORTANT

If a scientist uses AI to generate or manipulate text for a LinkedIn post, it is legally considered “published text” because it is accessible to a large, indeterminate number of readers.

item.title: 2 types of scientists and how they win
item.description:
research grants and awards.

Over the years, I’ve worked with and interviewed hundreds of scientists. And somewhere along the way, I started noticing a pattern - there are two types of scientists when it comes to communicating impact of their research.

Type 1 publishes in journals and goes to conferences. Everything beyond that is done half heartedly. Be it participating in public events liek open doors day or organising a summer school or posting on social media.

item.title: Two ways of science communication
item.description:
and why human angle always wins!

When creating content for science communication, you generally have two options:

  1. The Science Angle: You talk strictly about the research projects—focusing on scope, technical results, and future outlooks.
  2. The Human Angle: You focus on the scientist’s journey—their background, how they think, and the human story behind the discoveries.

At Under the Microscope*, we take the second, human angle. We put the scientist under the microscope, and through their personal and professional journey, we spotlight the incredible world of materials and nanoscience.

item.title: Difference between Communication and Dissemination
item.description:
relevant for you and your research proposals.

Communication and dissemination aren’t the same thing — and treating them separately is what makes your research stand out.

Communication builds your credibility over time. It’s broad and ongoing — papers, conference talks, the general visibility you build just by doing good research and showing up in your field.

Dissemination works differently. It’s the deliberate, targeted transfer of your research to specific audiences who can use it — think podcasts, videos, webinars, press releases.

item.title: New EU AI Act disclosures start Aug 2, 2026
item.description:
Are you ready for Article 50?

Hello helllooo,

The EU AI Act’s transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026 — and if you publish AI-generated content professionally, you have specific disclosure duties that go well beyond adding a footnote to your terms and conditions.

For the past two years I’ve been evaluating different AI tools and I just winged it when it came to disclosures. And so, honestly, I’m very happy to see these guidelines which will soon be regulations.

You’ve probably seen of “AI guidance for scientists” but have you heard of the “AI guidance for grant proposal evaluators”?!

The European Research Council, the largest European funding agency with € 17 billion budget, has FINALLY released “The use of AI in grant proposal evaluation” guidelines for ERC panel members and remote reviewers.

item.title: You're allowed to budget for your own development
item.description:
﻿Hello hellooo!

Can I tell you about something that almost every scientist misses when writing a funding proposal?

It’s not the science. It’s not the methodology. It’s not even the impact section (though yes, that too).

It’s the budget where you are actually allowed to invest in yourself.

Most proposals have a section for project management, coordination, or career development activities. It goes by different names depending on the funding scheme, but it is almost always there. And almost always, scientists either leave it vague, fill it with generic descriptions, or don’t use it at all.

item.description:

Sooo I’ve been thinking about what makes scientists happy.
And collaboration keeps coming up as the favourite aspect of being a scientist. Bringing different skills and resources together to tackle ambitious research problems brings back our childhood memories when we used to play together. It’s even better when this collaboration is well funded for longer periods of time, say 6 years.

This is exactly what ERC Synergy Grant are for. ERC is European Research Council and it gives grants up to €10 million (additional €4 million when justified) for 6 years to a team of scientists. Two to four principle investigators (PI) coming together and working towards a shared vision. It’s awesome!

item.title: How often should you post on LinkedIn?
item.description:

item.title: Mix and match AI tools for better results
item.description:
Three attempts, then switch—the rhythm that actually works

A few days ago, I was designing a carousel for a client. Claude understood the concept instantly, but after three attempts, it kept generating one Canva page instead of six. Rather than fighting with it or spending another hour tweaking prompts, I tried something simple — I switched tools. Within minutes, I had exactly what I needed.

Success with AI isn’t about becoming an expert in one tool or staying loyal to your favourite platform. It’s about adaptability—knowing when to switch, and which tool to switch to. This approach has completely changed how I use AI, especially when navigating the complex tasks that scientists, researchers, and science communicators face daily.

item.title: Do you know which AI tools you're actually allowed to use?
item.description:
Which tools you can use, what your funder requires, and where to find actual guidance

Hello there,

I’ve been having the same conversation with researchers across Europe for months now. It usually starts with: “Can I actually use ChatGPT for my grant proposal?” or “Is Claude allowed for literature reviews at my university?”

The answer is frustratingly complex: it depends on your institution, your funder, and sometimes even which department you’re in. One university bans commercial AI tools entirely whilst another actively encourages them. The ERC has guidelines, but they’re different from what your national funding agency requires.

item.title: The one AI tool scientists can use without institutional approval
item.description:
Why NotebookLM bypasses your university’s AI policy (plus: AI Labs is now part of our coverage)

Hello helllo!

Here’s what’s changing: Starting now, AI tools for scientists is part of our regular coverage. Not because AI is trendy, but because there’s a massive gap between what AI tools can do for researchers and what scientists are actually using—mostly due to institutional policy confusion, accuracy concerns, and data security fears. Over the past years, I’ve been quietly testing AI tools specifically for scientific workflows. Most are either unusable for serious research or violate institutional guidelines. But a few work brilliantly when used correctly.

item.title: How do you measure the success of your podcast?
item.description:
Beyond downloads - 1:10 Model, Performance, Impact

Podcasting is still new territory for many players in materials and nanoscience—funding agencies, research institutes, equipment manufacturers, and accelerators alike. But with no universal yardstick for success. How do you measure the success of a science podcast? The short answer: there’s no one-size-fits-all metric.

A good podcast isn’t just about downloads. It’s about strategy. It’s about impact. It’s about relevance.

In this edition, I’m sharing 3 performance indicators we use at Under the Microscope Podcast that might just help you build your own system for tracking podcast impact.

item.title: MALE Nobel laureate claimed ANTIMALE DISCRIMINATION
item.description:
Last week a Nobel laureate claimed ANTIMALE DISCRIMINATION at the Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings Yep, Antimale Discrimination.

I tried my best to stay out of it but this keeps coming up and I think this incidence has opened, yet again, a very important discussion.

I personally would like to believe that the old-white-man had good intentions as he is quoted in the article by Amanda Heidt saying that tokenising women in science is ridiculous. However, I think the message could and should have been packaged in a respectful way. More details and thoughts in the latest video of #ListenUp

item.title: 1K+ plays - woohoo!
item.description:
Under the Microscope podcast crossed 1k plays

Wanted to share the good news first with you all. Thank you for your continued love and support!

SciArt of the month - Feb 2023

This science art piece shows cell nuclei that contain DNA in the eye of a developing zebrafish. The nuclei were stained using DAPI staining that binds to the DNA, imaged with a state-of-the-art AiryScan microscope, and the images were subsequently processed. Using biomedical image analysis to extract, separate, and depth-code these data, we can start to see nuclei closer to the viewer in black, and those further away using an image gradient like red-green-blue-cyan-magenta and finally the yellow, which is furthest in the tissue. These data help us understand how the eye is formed. Check out more here: https://twitter.com/Zeeks_Art

item.title: Sleep & Cherries 😴🍒
item.description:
Happy Sunday!

New technology transforms our sleep into data. Sleep scores and hypnograms are telling me every day how good my watch perceived my sleep during the night. But what does good quality of sleep actually mean? And how can we accurately measure it? How much sleep is enough? And what have cherries got to do with it?

Let’s dive into the science of sleep with me and learn how a glass of cherry juice can save you a trip to the pharmacy and your disrupted night.

SciArt of the month

Virtual section through the eye of a developing zebrafish. The cells you see here are specialized glia cells called Müller Glia, which fulfil many important functions and link to neurons and blood vessels in the eye. The image you see shows Müller Glia contacting photo receptors on the top, their interaction zone with neurons as a band in the middle, and their contact region to blood vessels at the bottom.
